The Cape elephant shrew (Elephantulus edwardii) exhibits a resting metabolic rate that has been quantified through controlled respirometry trials. At a core body temperature of 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C], the maximum basal oxygen consumption of this small insectivore reaches approximately 54.28 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = approximately 54.28 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This relatively modest metabolic demand reflects the species' small body size and its adaptation to the semi-arid environments of the Western Cape region of South Africa. Field studies indicate that neonates emerge from the birth canal at a remarkably low mass; newborn pups typically weigh around 11.9 grams [Wwb = around 11.9 grams]. This altricial weight at parturition necessitates an extended period of intense maternal care, during which the pups remain dependent on the mother's milk for their initial growth and thermoregulatory needs. The combination of a low basal metabolic rate and a minimal initial body mass is thought to be an adaptive strategy for conserving energy in an unpredictable environment where food resources such as ants and termites can vary seasonally.

Reproductive output in the Cape elephant shrew is characterized by relatively small litters but a sustained frequency of breeding events throughout favorable periods. Females typically give birth to one or two pups per litter [N_R_i = one or two pups per litter], a clutch size that is typical among the Macroscelididae. At a core body temperature of 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C], a female may produce as many as two litters each year [F_R_i = two litters each year], maintaining this pace throughout much of her reproductive life. This annual reproductive investment is modest compared to similarly sized rodents, reflecting a slower life-history strategy. The gestation period itself lasts for 51 days [tg = 51 days] at that same maternal temperature, a duration that is proportionally long for a mammal of this size and likely contributes to the relatively advanced state of the neonates at birth compared to many eutherian mammals of equivalent mass at a temperature of 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C].

Postnatal development proceeds through a clearly defined sequence of milestones, with the timing of key transitions critical for understanding the species' life history. The nursing pup remains fully dependent on its mother for nutrition until the weaning process begins. Weaning, characterized by the cessation of lactation and the pup's transition to solid food, occurs at approximately 28 days after birth [tx = approximately 28 days after birth] at the mother's core temperature of 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C]. This relatively early weaning age for a mammal of this body size allows the female to recover her energetic reserves and potentially initiate a subsequent pregnancy sooner. The juvenile then enters a prolonged sub-adult phase during which it must forage independently and develop the skills necessary for survival in a challenging environment. The growth trajectory from a neonatal mass of around 11.9 grams [Wwb = around 11.9 grams] to adult dimensions requires a sustained intake of invertebrate prey, primarily termites and ants.

Sexual maturity in the Cape elephant shrew is a delayed process relative to the weaning age, a pattern that underscores the species' conservative life-history strategy. Puberty, defined as the onset of gonadal activity, is reached at 330 days after birth [tp = 330 days after birth] at a slightly cooler core body temperature of 36.3 °C [T = 36.3 °C]. This nearly year-long interval from parturition to reproductive activation is unusual among small insectivorous mammals and suggests that significant physiological or somatic preparation is required before a female can undertake the energetic demands of gestation and lactation. The ultimate adult body mass attained by females, a key determinant of reproductive potential, reaches approximately 50 grams [Wwi = approximately 50 grams]. This asymptotic mass is reached only after several months of post-weaning growth, during which the juvenile must accumulate sufficient fat reserves and skeletal mass to support future breeding efforts in the face of seasonal resource fluctuations.

Longevity records for the Cape elephant shrew, largely inferred from comparative data on the closely related Elephantulus intufi, indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 4.2 years [am = approximately 4.2 years] at a stable core body temperature of 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C]. This lifespan, combined with a late age at first reproduction and small litter sizes, places the species firmly within a slow life-history continuum. Such a strategy is consistent with the relatively low extrinsic mortality rates typical of small mammals inhabiting stable, arid environments where predation pressure may be buffered by cryptic behavior and nocturnal activity. The integration of these demographic parameters — a lifespan of over four years, a late sexual maturation at nearly a full year after birth, and a reproductive rate limited to modest litter sizes — paints a picture of a species finely tuned to persist in a challenging landscape through iteroparity and prolonged somatic investment rather than through high fecundity.
